title: A prospective, randomized study investigating the effectiveness of extracorporeal shock wave therapy and radiotherapy in the treatment of refractory, symptomatic heel spur and plantar fasciitis
summary:
Many people experience heel pain at some point in their lives due to heel spurs or inflammation of the sole of the foot. These complaints can have a significant impact on quality of life. Simple measures such as painkillers, stretching exercises, or insoles for shoes often help. However, if the pain persists, treatment is difficult and it is unclear which therapy works best.

Two commonly used options are very low-dose radiation therapy and shock wave treatment. Both methods do not require surgery and have been shown in studies to relieve pain and improve mobility. They are also generally well tolerated. However, there are no studies to date that directly compare the two methods.

A new study will now investigate which of the two treatments is more effective. The main focus will be on how much the pain is reduced and whether patients can use their foot better again. In addition, the study will record how patients experience the treatment overall, how their quality of life changes, whether further therapies are necessary, whether they need less medication, whether they regret their decision, and whether side effects occur. A new German questionnaire on these foot complaints will also be tested.

Radiation therapy consists of six short treatments over a period of two weeks. If the symptoms have not improved after three months, the therapy can be repeated once. Shock wave therapy is performed on three occasions, each one week apart. The aim of this study is to compare the two procedures fairly and thus find out which treatment is most beneficial for patients with persistent heel pain.

interventions.name: Patients receiving low-dose radiation therapy (6 sessions of 0.5 Gy, 3 sessions per week).
Patients receiving extracorporeal shock wave therapy (3 sessions, sessions at weekly intervals).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Clinical evidence of plantar fasciitis with symptoms lasting ≥ 6 months
Typical clinical symptoms with tenderness on palpation
Treatment-resistant symptoms with no response to pharmacological and non-pharmacological measures, including patient-centered measures (including at least rest, stretching exercises, and insoles). 
Typical functional deficit: limitation of pain-free walking distance
Karnofsky Performance Index ≥ 70%
Written patient consent to participate in the study (informed consent)
Exclusion criteria:
Previous radiation therapy or extracorporeal shock wave therapy on the affected foot within the last 12 months
Previous trauma to the affected foot (e.g., fracture, tendon rupture)
Active rheumatoid arthritis
Symptomatic peripheral arterial occlusive disease
Severe venous insufficiency
Manifest lymphedema in the affected limb
Pregnancy, breastfeeding
Severe psychiatric illness
Legal guardianship in medical matters by third parties
